title: King Hui of Liang, Part I

verses.t: Mencius went to see King Hui of Liang. The king said, "Venerable sir, you have not thought a thousand li too far to come. Surely you have something that will profit my state?" Mencius replied, "Why must Your Majesty speak of profit? There is only humaneness and righteousness. If the king says, 'How can I profit my state?', the great officers say, 'How can I profit my family?', and the scholars and common people say, 'How can I profit myself?', then high and low will be grasping for profit from one another, and the state will be in danger. In a state of ten thousand chariots, the one who murders its ruler will surely be [the head of] a family of a thousand chariots; in a state of a thousand chariots, the one who murders its ruler will surely be [the head of] a family of a hundred chariots. A thousand out of ten thousand, or a hundred out of a thousand, is no small share. But if righteousness is put last and profit first, they will not be satisfied until they have seized everything. There has never been a humane man who abandoned his parents, nor a righteous man who put his ruler last. Let Your Majesty speak only of humaneness and righteousness. Why must you speak of profit?"

Mencius went to see King Hui of Liang. The king was standing beside his pond, looking round at the wild geese and the deer, and he said, "Do worthy men also take pleasure in these things?" Mencius replied, "Only worthy men can take pleasure in them. Those who are not worthy, even if they have such things, cannot enjoy them. The Book of Odes says: 'He began to plan the Spirit Tower; he planned it and laid it out. The common people worked at it, and in less than a day they finished it. He began to plan it, saying, "Do not hurry," but the common people came like children. The king was in the Spirit Park, where the does lay at rest; the does were sleek and glossy, the white birds gleaming. The king was by the Spirit Pond; how full it was of leaping fish!' King Wen used the people's labor to build his tower and his pond, yet the people delighted in them. They called his tower the Spirit Tower and his pond the Spirit Pond, and they rejoiced that he had deer, fish and turtles. The men of antiquity shared their pleasures with the people, and that is why they could enjoy them. The Declaration of Tang says: 'When will this sun perish? We would perish together with you!' When the people wish to perish together with their ruler, then even if he has towers and ponds, birds and beasts, how can he enjoy them alone?"

King Hui of Liang said, "In governing my state, I give it my whole heart. When the harvest fails in Henei, I move people to Hedong and send grain to Henei. When the harvest fails in Hedong, I do the same. When I look at the government of neighboring states, none of their rulers takes such pains as I do. Yet the people of neighboring states do not grow fewer, and my people do not grow more numerous. Why is that?" Mencius replied, "Your Majesty loves war, so let me use war as an illustration. The drums roll, the blades meet, and then soldiers throw off their armor and run, dragging their weapons behind them. Some stop after a hundred paces, some after fifty. If those who ran fifty paces laughed at those who ran a hundred, what would you think of that?" The king said, "They would be wrong. They simply did not run a hundred paces; they ran all the same." Mencius said, "If Your Majesty understands this, then do not hope that your people will become more numerous than those of neighboring states. If the farming seasons are not interfered with, there will be more grain than can be eaten. If fine-meshed nets are not allowed into the pools and ponds, there will be more fish and turtles than can be eaten. If axes enter the hills and forests only at the proper season, there will be more timber than can be used. When there is more grain, fish and turtles than can be eaten, and more timber than can be used, the people can nourish their living and bury their dead without regret. That the people can nourish their living and bury their dead without regret is the beginning of the true king's way. Let mulberry trees be planted around homesteads of five mu, and those who are fifty can wear silk. Let chickens, pigs and dogs be raised without missing their breeding seasons, and those who are seventy can eat meat. Let fields of a hundred mu not be robbed of their seasons, and a family of several mouths need not go hungry. Pay careful attention to teaching in the schools, and impress on the people the duties of filial and brotherly devotion, and grey-haired people will not be seen carrying loads on their backs and heads along the roads. When those of seventy wear silk and eat meat, and the common people suffer neither hunger nor cold, there has never been a ruler who failed in such a case to become a true king. But now your dogs and pigs eat the people's food and you do not think to restrain them; people are dying of hunger on the roads and you do not think to open the granaries. When people die, you say, 'It was not I; it was the harvest.' How is that different from stabbing a man to death and saying, 'It was not I; it was the weapon'? If Your Majesty stops blaming the harvest, the people of the whole world will come to you."

King Hui of Liang said, "I would gladly receive your instruction." Mencius replied, "Is there any difference between killing a man with a club and killing him with a blade?" "There is no difference." "Is there any difference between killing him with a blade and killing him with government?" "There is no difference." Mencius said, "In your kitchen there is fat meat and in your stables there are fat horses, yet the people look hungry, and in the countryside lie those who have starved to death. This is leading animals to devour people. Even when animals devour one another, people hate it. If one who is father and mother to the people governs in such a way that he cannot avoid leading animals to devour people, where is his being father and mother to the people? Zhongni said, 'The man who first made wooden figures [for burials], surely he will have no descendants!' That was because he made images of people and used them [in the grave]. What then of making these people die of hunger?"

King Hui of Liang said, "There was once no state in the world stronger than Jin, as you, venerable sir, know. But in my own time we were defeated by Qi in the east, and my eldest son died there; in the west we lost seven hundred li of land to Qin; and in the south we were humiliated by Chu. I am ashamed of this, and for the sake of those who died I wish to wash away the disgrace once and for all. How can it be done?" Mencius replied, "With a territory of only a hundred li square one can become a true king. If Your Majesty practises humane government toward the people, is sparing with punishments, lightens taxes and levies, so that the fields are plowed deep and weeded well, and the able-bodied men use their spare days to cultivate filial devotion, brotherly respect, loyalty and good faith, serving their fathers and elder brothers at home and their elders and superiors abroad, then you could have them take up mere sticks and beat back the strong armor and sharp weapons of Qin and Chu. Those rulers rob their people of their time, so that they cannot plow and weed to support their parents. Their parents freeze and starve; brothers, wives and children are parted and scattered. Those rulers have plunged their people into pits and drowned them. If Your Majesty goes and punishes them, who will oppose you? Hence it is said, 'The humane man has no enemy.' I beg Your Majesty not to doubt it."

Mencius had an audience with King Xiang of Liang. When he came out, he said to someone, "Seen from a distance, he does not look like a ruler; close up, I saw nothing in him that commands respect. He asked me abruptly, 'How can the world be settled?' I replied, 'It will be settled by being united.' 'Who can unite it?' I replied, 'One who has no taste for killing people can unite it.' 'Who will give it to him?' I replied, 'There is no one in the world who will not give it to him. Does Your Majesty know about young grain? If there is drought in the seventh and eighth months, the young plants wither. Then Heaven gathers thick clouds and sends down rain in torrents, and the plants spring up vigorously. When it is like this, who can hold them back? Now among the shepherds of men in the world there is not one who has no taste for killing people. If there were one who had no taste for killing people, then all the people of the world would stretch out their necks to look for him. If it were truly so, the people would turn to him as water flows downward, in a flood; who could hold it back?'"

King Xuan of Qi asked, "May I hear about the deeds of Duke Huan of Qi and Duke Wen of Jin?" Mencius replied, "None of the followers of Zhongni spoke of the deeds of Huan and Wen, and so nothing about them has been handed down to later ages. I have not heard of them. If I must speak, shall it be about true kingship?" "What must one's virtue be like for one to become a true king?" "Protect the people and become a true king, and no one can stop you." "Can someone like me protect the people?" "You can." "How do you know that I can?" "I heard from Hu He that Your Majesty was sitting up in the hall when someone led an ox past below. Seeing it, Your Majesty said, 'Where is the ox going?' The man replied, 'It is to be used to consecrate a bell with its blood.' Your Majesty said, 'Let it go. I cannot bear its trembling, like an innocent man being led to the place of death.' He replied, 'Then shall we give up consecrating the bell?' Your Majesty said, 'How can that be given up? Use a sheep instead.' I do not know whether this happened." "It did." "This heart is enough to make you a true king. The people all thought Your Majesty was being stingy, but I know for certain that it was because you could not bear it." The king said, "Yes, there really were people who thought so. Though Qi is a small and narrow state, how could I grudge a single ox? It was simply that I could not bear its trembling, like an innocent man being led to the place of death, and so I replaced it with a sheep." Mencius said, "Do not wonder that the people thought Your Majesty stingy. You replaced a large animal with a small one; how were they to know [your reason]? If Your Majesty was pained at its going innocent to the place of death, then what was there to choose between an ox and a sheep?" The king laughed and said, "What was really in my heart, then? It was not that I grudged the cost, and yet I replaced it with a sheep. No wonder the people said I was stingy." Mencius said, "There is no harm in it. This was precisely the working of humaneness: you had seen the ox but not the sheep. The gentleman's attitude toward animals is this: having seen them alive, he cannot bear to see them die; having heard their cries, he cannot bear to eat their flesh. That is why the gentleman keeps his distance from the kitchen." The king said, "The Book of Odes says: 'Others have their thoughts; I can fathom them.' That describes you, Master. I was the one who did it, yet when I turned and looked for my reason, I could not find my own heart. When you spoke of it, Master, my heart was deeply stirred. But how is it that this heart accords with true kingship?" Mencius said, "Suppose someone reported to Your Majesty, 'My strength is enough to lift a hundred jun, but not enough to lift a single feather; my sight is sharp enough to see the tip of an autumn hair, but I cannot see a cartload of firewood.' Would Your Majesty accept that?" "No." "Now your kindness is enough to reach the animals, yet its benefits do not reach the people. Why is that alone so? The feather is not lifted because strength is not used; the cartload of firewood is not seen because sight is not used; the people are not protected because kindness is not used. So Your Majesty's not becoming a true king comes from not doing it, not from being unable." "How do the forms of not doing and of being unable differ?" "If a man is told to tuck Mount Tai under his arm and leap over the North Sea, and he tells people, 'I cannot,' that is truly being unable. If he is told to bend a branch for an elder, and he tells people, 'I cannot,' that is not doing it, not being unable. So Your Majesty's not becoming a true king is not like tucking Mount Tai under one's arm and leaping over the North Sea; it is like bending a branch. Treat your own aged as the aged should be treated, and extend this to the aged of others; treat your own young as the young should be treated, and extend this to the young of others; then the world can be turned in the palm of your hand. The Book of Odes says: 'He set an example for his wife, extended it to his brothers, and so governed his clan and his state.' That is to say, he simply took this heart and applied it to others. So if one extends one's kindness, it is enough to protect all within the four seas; if one does not extend it, one cannot protect even one's wife and children. The reason the ancients far surpassed other men was nothing else than this: they were good at extending what they did. Now your kindness is enough to reach the animals, yet its benefits do not reach the people. Why is that alone so? Weigh a thing, and then you know whether it is light or heavy; measure it, and then you know whether it is long or short. All things are so, and the heart most of all. I beg Your Majesty to measure it. Or is it that only when Your Majesty raises armies, puts your officers and ministers in danger, and stirs up enmity among the feudal lords, does your heart feel satisfied?" The king said, "No. How could I take satisfaction in that? I do it in order to seek what I greatly desire." "May I hear what it is that Your Majesty greatly desires?" The king smiled and did not speak. Mencius said, "Is it that you do not have enough rich and sweet food for your mouth? Or light and warm clothing for your body? Or is it that you do not have enough bright colors for your eyes to look at, or music for your ears to hear, or favorites to wait on you and take your orders? Your Majesty's ministers can supply all of these. Surely Your Majesty is not doing it for these?" "No, I am not doing it for these." "Then what Your Majesty greatly desires can be known. You wish to enlarge your territory, to have Qin and Chu come to your court, to rule over the Central States and to pacify the barbarians on all four sides. But to seek what you desire by such means is like climbing a tree to look for fish." The king said, "Is it as bad as that?" "It is probably worse. If you climb a tree to look for fish, you get no fish, but no disaster follows. If you seek what you desire by such means, and pour all your heart and strength into it, disaster is sure to follow." "May I hear why?" "If the people of Zou fought the people of Chu, who does Your Majesty think would win?" "The people of Chu would win." "So the small certainly cannot match the large, the few certainly cannot match the many, and the weak certainly cannot match the strong. Within the seas there are nine territories of a thousand li square, and Qi, all its lands put together, has one of them. For one to try to subdue the other eight, how is that different from Zou taking on Chu? Why not go back to the root? If Your Majesty now issues a government that practises humaneness, then all in the world who hold office will wish to stand in Your Majesty's court, all who plow will wish to plow in Your Majesty's fields, all merchants will wish to store their goods in Your Majesty's markets, all travelers will wish to go by Your Majesty's roads, and all in the world who resent their own rulers will wish to come and lay their complaints before Your Majesty. If it is like that, who can stop you?" The king said, "I am dull and cannot advance to this. I hope, Master, that you will help me toward my aim and teach me plainly. Though I am not quick, let me try." Mencius said, "Only a scholar can keep a constant heart without a constant livelihood. As for the common people, if they have no constant livelihood, they will consequently have no constant heart. And if they have no constant heart, there is nothing they will not do in the way of license, depravity, wickedness and extravagance. Then when they have fallen into crime, to go after them and punish them is to set a trap for the people. How can a humane man in high position set traps for the people? Therefore an enlightened ruler regulates the people's livelihood so that, looking up, they have enough to serve their parents, and looking down, enough to support their wives and children; so that in good years they always have their fill, and in bad years they escape death. Only then does he urge them toward goodness, and so the people follow him easily. But now the people's livelihood is so regulated that, looking up, they do not have enough to serve their parents, and looking down, not enough to support their wives and children; in good years their life is always bitter, and in bad years they do not escape death. They are only trying to save themselves from death and fear they will not manage it; what leisure do they have to cultivate ritual and righteousness? If Your Majesty wishes to put this into practice, why not go back to the root? Let mulberry trees be planted around homesteads of five mu, and those who are fifty can wear silk. Let chickens, pigs and dogs be raised without missing their breeding seasons, and those who are seventy can eat meat. Let fields of a hundred mu not be robbed of their seasons, and a family of eight mouths need not go hungry. Pay careful attention to teaching in the schools, and impress on the people the duty of filial and brotherly devotion, and grey-haired people will not be seen carrying loads on their backs and heads along the roads. When the old wear silk and eat meat, and the common people suffer neither hunger nor cold, there has never been a ruler who failed in such a case to become a true king."
